name: Nikhil Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for having me, Nikhil. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say is confidential, so you can tell me your public line and, separately, what you really think. To start, what's a normal working day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for my uncle Raj's firm, Quinn Building, five of us, in the market town where I grew up. We do extensions, loft conversions and the odd new house, and I'm mostly on the roofs: cutting rafters, fitting joists, building the frame for the dormers. I'm out of the house by quarter to seven in my pickup, which is paid off, and we're usually on someone's driveway by half past. My uncle still works out the roof angles with a pencil and a steel square, and so do I.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you love about it, and what's tough?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love standing on a ridge at lunch and seeing the whole town, the church spire and the river. I know half the customers from church or school, so the work feels like it matters. The tough part is the weather and my shoulders, and customers who've watched a home renovation show and think a loft takes a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's what I'd expect. A lot of noise from people who've never held a hammer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: you can't download a roof. People round here trust the person, not the gadget. I'm not online much, but I'd say it in the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means nothing changes, which is good. I've got savings, the pickup's mine, and Priya and I are getting married at St Mary's next summer. I don't use AI and I don't plan to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. Keep working with Raj, keep saving for the wedding and a deposit. If the AI helped Raj's accountant with the books, fine, that's his business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a dry week on a roof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why don't you use those tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't trust things I can't see inside. My uncle taught me to check every cut twice, and you can't check a computer's thinking. My phone does calls and the football scores, that's enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone in town you'd worry about even here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Maybe the bank, they're always closing branches anyway. But that's not AI, that's just greed.

S0.say: I'd say you can't download a roof, and people round here trust the person, not the gadget. I'm not online much, but I'd say it in the pub.
S0.think: Nothing changes, which suits him: he has savings, a paid-off pickup and a church wedding planned next summer. He doesn't use AI and has no plans to.
S0.do: Carries on working at his uncle's firm and keeps saving for the wedding and a house deposit. Leaves any AI use to the firm's accountant.
S0.feel: Calm, like a dry week on a roof.
S0.quote: My uncle taught me to check every cut twice, and you can't check a computer's thinking.
S0.fieldNote: Nikhil is rooted in a family firm, a small town and his church. His distrust of AI is practical and moral at once: he wants to see inside what he relies on. A plateau confirms his worldview.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hm. A few years of that. I think we'd be all right in a town like ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say small firms like ours will be fine because people want someone they know on their roof. I'd say good luck to the big companies if they want to try. And I'd say young lads should still learn a trade, not sit at a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the big housing developers might use factory roofs and machines, and that could squeeze prices. But extensions and lofts are fiddly, every house is different. I think we'd keep going, maybe with a bit less margin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing much, honestly. Keep working, keep saving for the wedding. If Raj wanted to buy some new kit I'd let him, and I'd learn it slowly if I had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A little cloud on the horizon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you change your mind about learning the new kit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Raj told me to. He's my uncle and my boss. If he says the firm needs it, I'd learn it, grumbling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who should help the people whose jobs shrink?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Families and churches first, and employers training people up. I don't want everyone living off the state. Apprenticeships, that's how my dad got his start and how I got mine.

S1.say: I'd say small firms will be fine because people want someone they know on their roof, and young people should still learn a trade, not sit at a screen.
S1.think: Big developers might use factory roofs and machines and squeeze prices, but fiddly extensions and lofts will keep the firm going, maybe on thinner margins.
S1.do: Keeps working and saving for the wedding. Lets his uncle buy new kit if he wants and learns it slowly if he has to.
S1.feel: Mostly calm, with a little cloud on the horizon.
S1.quote: If he says the firm needs it, I'd learn it, grumbling.
S1.fieldNote: Nikhil trusts the small-town, personal nature of his work to protect him. His views on support are firmly traditional: family, church, employers and apprenticeships before the state. He'd only adopt technology on his uncle's say-so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Robots on roofs. That's a different story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is what happens when we let tech companies run everything. Somebody should have put the brakes on, and I'd want to know who let it happen. I'd say people should look after their own and their neighbours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be frightened. Roofing is just measuring, cutting and fixing, and if a robot can do all three without getting tired, the firm's done. I'd be twenty-nine with no other skill, about to start a family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut back hard, straight away. We'd make the wedding smaller, maybe just the church and a meal at Priya's parents', and put the money we save in the bank instead. I'd keep working while Raj still had jobs, and lean on my family and the church community if it got bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like the ladder slipping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're not keen on state support. Would you take it here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I had to, I'd take it, and I'd hate it. But I'd go to family first. My dad would say the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Priya?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we're still getting married, even if it's twenty people in a church hall. That's the bit that doesn't change. The house might have to wait.

S2.say: I'd say this is what happens when tech companies run everything and nobody puts the brakes on, and I'd want to know who let it happen. People should look after their own and their neighbours.
S2.think: He'd be frightened, because roofing is measuring, cutting and fixing, and a tireless robot doing all three would finish the firm. He'd be 29 with no other skill, about to start a family.
S2.do: Cuts back hard straight away, shrinking the wedding to the church and a meal and banking the difference. Keeps working while his uncle has jobs, and leans on family and church if things get bad.
S2.quote: That we're still getting married, even if it's twenty people in a church hall.
S2.fieldNote: Nikhil blames tech companies and a lack of brakes, but his solutions are family and faith rather than politics. He'd accept state help only reluctantly. The wedding is the thing he protects, even as the house deposit slips.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay. Still fast, but there's a bit of a run-up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so families should get their houses in order, literally. Pay off debts, save, look after each other. I'd say that at church and at the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think five years means I'd get the wedding and maybe a house done before it hits. I'd be thirty-two. I'd still be worried, because I don't know what I'd do after roofs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save everything I could and get the house bought quickly, then pay off as much of the mortgage as possible. I'd keep working with Raj the same as now. If he got a robot, I suppose I'd learn to run it, but I wouldn't go looking for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, but I'd think about it on the roof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why rush to buy a house, if work might go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because then it's ours. A house paid down is something no machine can take off you. My grandparents owned their house outright by fifty and it got them through everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you look at any other work in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not. I'm not one for jumping around. I'd stick with Raj and trust that we'd sort something out together.

S3.say: I'd say there are a few years, so families should get their houses in order: pay off debts, save and look after each other. I'd say it at church and in the pub.
S3.think: Five years means the wedding and maybe a house would be done before it hits, and he'd be 32. He'd still be worried because he doesn't know what he'd do after roofing.
S3.do: Saves all he can, buys a house quickly and overpays the mortgage. Keeps working with his uncle and would only learn to run a robot if the firm got one.
S3.feel: Anxious but not panicking, thinking about it while up on the roof.
S3.quote: A house paid down is something no machine can take off you.
S3.fieldNote: His response to more time is to anchor himself in property and family rather than new skills. He wouldn't look for other work, trusting his uncle's firm. Ownership, as his grandparents had, is his idea of safety.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's more like it. I'd be thirty-seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time for people to prepare themselves, and they shouldn't wait for the government to do it. Train young people, support families, keep communities strong. That's what I'd say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd be okay. Ten years of work and saving, a house mostly paid off, maybe kids by then. The worry is what my kids would do, not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working with Raj, buy the house, keep saving every month. If Raj retired I might take over the firm, which I've half thought about anyway. I'd carry on as normal and keep an eye on things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. But ten years is a long time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take over the firm, knowing AGI arrives in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. I'd have eight or nine good years from it. And people round here might still want the Quinn name on their roof for a while, even if a robot's doing the nailing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your kids, if you had them by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn something with your hands and something with your head. And go to church, because community is what gets you through. That's what my mum told me.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty of time for people to prepare themselves without waiting for government. Train young people, support families and keep communities strong.
S4.think: He'd probably be okay, with ten years of work and saving and a house mostly paid off, maybe children by then. His worry would be about his children's future, not his own.
S4.do: Keeps working with his uncle, buys the house and keeps saving monthly. Might take over the firm if his uncle retires.
S4.feel: Uneasy, but ten years feels like a long time.
S4.quote: People round here might still want the Quinn name on their roof for a while, even if a robot's doing the nailing.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Nikhil's thinking shifts to his future children and the family firm. He'd stay with what he knows and maybe take over the business. Community and church remain his safety net.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd have no time to get the house and the wedding done. What would help is apprenticeships and support for small family firms, so we can keep people working, and churches and communities that actually look after their own.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether people would still care who built their house. I hope they would. I've fixed roofs over people I went to Sunday school with, and that has to count for something.

headlineQuote: I've fixed roofs over people I went to Sunday school with, and that has to count for something.
portrait: Nikhil Quinn is a 27-year-old roofing and framing carpenter at his uncle's five-person firm in the market town where he grew up, engaged to Priya with a church wedding planned next summer. He has strong savings, a paid-off pickup, and never uses AI, trusting a pencil and steel square instead. He stays calm in the mild pictures, convinced people want someone they know on their roof. The two-year AGI picture alarms him and he'd shrink the wedding and lean on family and church; with more time he'd buy a house, pay it down and maybe take over the firm.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because he'd have no time to get the house and wedding done before roofing work disappeared.
whatWouldHelp: Apprenticeships and support for small family firms to keep people working, and churches and communities that look after their own.
